articles.title: Will Venable, Pat Murphy Win AL, NL Manager Year 2026 Awards, Full MLB Voting Results
articles.summary: After leading their respective teams to historic seasons, Milwaukee Brewers manager Pat Murphy and Chicago White Sox manager Will Venable received some new hardware to recognize their efforts.
articles.body:
After leading their respective teams to historic seasons, Milwaukee Brewers manager Pat Murphy and Chicago White Sox manager Will Venable received some new hardware to recognize their efforts.

Murphy has made history by winning his third consecutive NL Manager of the Year award after leading the Brewers to their first championship in franchise history.

Meanwhile, after leading the White Sox to a historic turnaround, Venable has been rewarded for his efforts with the 2026 AL Manager of the Year award.

Venable received 15 first-place votes and 111 total points from the BBWAA voting to finish ahead of Kevin Cash of the Tampa Bay Rays and Chad Tracy of the Boston Red Sox.

There were nine managers in MLB history who have won Manager of the Year at least three times, but none of them had ever done it consecutively until Murphy.

The 67-year-old Murphy, already regarded as perhaps the best manager in MLB coming into 2026, put together arguably his best season. He led the Brewers to a franchise-record 103 wins during the regular season.

It was the second straight year that Milwaukee has set a franchise record for wins after going 97-65 in 2025.

Murphy and the Brewers carried that positive momentum into the playoffs. They put together an 11-2 overall record that saw them win eight straight games between Game 4 of the NLDS through Game 3 of the World Series, tied with the 2014 Kansas City Royals and 2004 Boston Red Sox for the. longest streak in a single postseason.

The Brewers promoted Murphy to their managerial position in November 2023 after Craig Counsell left to take the same job with the Chicago Cubs. He has won the NL Manager of the Year every season he has been in the position.

Murphy was just one of four managers in MLB history to win back-to-back Manager of the Year awards with his victories in 2024 and 2025.

Bobby Cox of the Atlanta Braves (2004-05), Kevin Cash of the Tampa Bay Rays (2020-21) and Stephen Vogt of the Cleveland Guardians (2024-25) were the others.

With a third NL Manager of the Year award on his mantle, Murphy joins a group that includes Cox, Tony La Russa, Terry Francona, Dusty Baker, Buck Showalter, Lou Piniella, Joe Maddon, Bob Melvin and Jim Leyland as the only skippers to win the award at least three times.

Venable was originally hired by the White Sox after the 2024 season when the team set a new MLB record with 121 losses.

Chicago's first season under Venable didn't immediately stand out with a 60-102 record, but it was a 19-game improvement from the previous year.

Thanks in part to improved play from homegrown talent and outside acquisitions, most notably signing Munetaka Murakami, Venable led the White Sox to an 84-78 record in 2026 and their first playoff berth in five years.

The White Sox became the first team in MLB history to make the playoffs coming off at least two consecutive 100-loss seasons.

The White Sox first moved into first place in the AL Central on June 10, marking their first time in sole possession of the top spot in the division since April 17, 2022.

Even though the White Sox would eventually cede control of the AL Central to the Cleveland Guardians in the final weekend of the regular season, they clinched a playoff berth on Sept. 24 with a win over the Kansas City Royals.

Chicago won its first four playoff games, sweeping the Houston Astros in the AL Wild Card series and taking a 2-0 lead in the ALDS over Cleveland, to get within one win of reaching the ALCS.

The Guardians won three straight to close out the series, but Chicago's season was nothing short of a resounding success that has its future very bright.

Venable is the sixth White Sox skipper to win AL Manager of the Year. He joins past winners Tony La Russa (1983), Jeff Torborg (1990), Gene Lamont (1993), Jerry Manuel (2000) and Ozzie Guillén (2005).

articles.title: Elly De La Cruz Trade Buzz Addressed by Reds President Amid 2026 MLB Free Agency
articles.summary: Cincinnati Reds president of baseball operations, Nick Krall, told reporters on Tuesday that the Reds "haven't had any conversations" about Elly De La Cruz this offseason with other teams but added he's "never going to say never."
articles.body:
Cincinnati Reds president of baseball operations, Nick Krall, told reporters on Tuesday that the Reds "haven't had any conversations" about Elly De La Cruz this offseason with other teams but added he's "never going to say never."

"We have three years of control," Krall added . "He's a really good player on our club. If there's something out there and someone wants to come to us and talk about it—he's a great player and I love having him on our team."

De La Cruz, 24, is the face of the Reds and one of the most exciting young players in the sport. The two-time All-Star hit .283 with 30 homers, 79 RBI, 99 runs, 30 stolen bases and a .880 OPS in 2026 and just about every contender in the sport likely would be calling Krall if there was any possibility of De La Cruz being moved.

Thus far, that seems incredibly unlikely. Granted, De La Cruz may eventually grow weary of Cincinnati's mediocrity, with the team only registering one playoff berth in his four seasons and a 317-331 record in that time.

But for now, the Reds have little incentive to trade the most exciting player they've had in years.

articles.title: Will Venable wins AL Manager of the Year award after huge turnaround with White Sox
articles.summary: The White Sox improved by 24 games in 2026.
articles.body:
The Chicago White Sox won 60 games in Will Venable's first season as manager. One year later, the team had a two-game lead in the ALDS before its fairytale season came to an end.

Because of that, Venable was named the 2026 American League Manager of the Year on Tuesday. He beat Tampa Bay Rays skipper Kevin Cash and Boston Red Sox manager Chad Tracy as finalists for the honor.

While Cash led the Rays to an AL-best 98 wins and Tracy saved the Red Sox from an abysmal 10-17 start, voters went with the man responsible for the biggest turnaround in baseball in 2026.

The White Sox improved their win total by 24 games from 2025 and finished second in the AL Central after leading the division for much of the year. The team came into the 2026 season expected to finish last in the division.

Venable played a pretty significant role in the White Sox's resurgence, particularly on the pitching side. In order to get the most out of a shaky rotation, he showed a willingness to utilize openers and bullpen games to give his team an edge.

Venable is the sixth White Sox manager to win the award, joining Ozzie Guillen (2005), Jerry Manuel (2000), Gene Lamont (1993), Jeff Torborg (1990) and Tony LaRussa (1983).

While Venable benefitted from the team's collective breakout on offense, he also utilized platoons to put players in the best spots to succeed. And it worked: One year after finishing 14th in the AL in runs scored, the White Sox led the league with 776 runs scored in 2026.

MLB collects its end-of-year votes ahead of the postseason, but even so, Venable put those same skills on display during the team's surprising playoff run. The White Sox won their first four postseason games, sweeping the Astros in the wild-card round and going up 2-0 on the Guardians in the ALDS, despite using a conventional starter just once in that stretch. The Guardians went on to win that series 3-2.

With Venable at the helm, the White Sox are poised to have even more success in the years to come. After proving himself in 2026, Venable will be out to show that he and the White Sox are the real deal in 2027.

articles.title: Pat Murphy wins unprecedented third straight NL Manager of the Year award after Brewers' World Series title
articles.summary: The Brewers' manager accepted the award from a hospital bed.
articles.body:
Milwaukee Brewers manager Pat Murphy is officially 3-for-3 when it comes to NL Manager of the Year. But that wasn't his biggest accomplishment this season.

Two weeks after leading Milwaukee to the franchise's first World Series title , Murphy became the first manager in MLB history to win a Manager of the Year Award in three straight seasons. Only two other managers, Bobby Cox (2004-05) and Kevin Cash (2020-21), had ever won twice in a row.

Notably, the 67-year-old Murphy accepted the award from a hospital bed, telling MLB Network that he had recently undergone hip replacement surgery.

Murphy received 20 of 30 first-place votes from the BBWAA, beating finalists Don Mattingly of the Philadelphia Phillies and Walt Weiss of the Atlanta Braves . Weiss finished second, with seven first-place votes, while Mattingly got one first-place vote and fourth-place finisher Craig Stammen of the San Diego Padres got two, both from the San Diego chapter.

All votes are submitted at the end of the regular season, meaning the Brewers' postseason success did not factor into the voting. Murphy won on the strength of a regular season in which the Brewers won a franchise-record 103 games .

No Brewers manager in club history had won a Manager of the Year award before Murphy's first season in 2024. Since then, Murphy has received 74 of 90 first-place Manager of the Year votes in the NL.

Pat Murphy's tenure as Brewers manager has been a golden age for the club

Murphy's tenure began under inauspicious circumstances. The position was available after then-Brewers manager Craig Counsell, a Wisconsin native and one of the game's most respected skippers, left Milwaukee in free agency to join the division-rival Chicago Cubs on a record contract . Few people in Wisconsin were happy about that .

The Brewers opted to replace Counsell by promoting his bench coach, Murphy . Up to that point, Murphy's coaching experience consisted of decades in the college ranks (which ended under a cloud of sanctions at Arizona State), assorted assistant jobs with the Brewers and San Diego Padres, and an interim stint with the Padres during which the club went 42-54. In the early 1990s, Murphy coached Counsell at Notre Dame.

At this point, it's impossible to argue that the Brewers aren't enjoying the better end of that divorce.

Milwaukee won 92 games in Counsell's final season in 2023, with their playoff run ending via a two-game sweep in the wild-card round. Despite an upheaval in talent on both the roster and in the front office, the Brewers won 93 games the next year. In 2025, they won 97 games and reached the NLCS. And, of course, 2026 went better than they could have possibly hoped.

Murphy has received plenty of credit for that renaissance, in which the small-market Brewers have adapted in an ever-changing game. Their roster was clearly built with intent, from a lineup that led MLB in walks to a bullpen willing to pitch whatever innings are needed. The Brewers embraced old-school facets of the game such as bunting and stealing bases while also employing openers and platoons to cover the roster's soft spots.

It was on Murphy to make all of that work. He obviously succeeded.

It's probably time to stop underestimating the Brewers

As happy as anyone is to win a trophy, the Manager of the Year awards can land as a backhanded compliment.

After all, voters don't know what's happening in every clubhouse. It's hard for a voter in one market to properly judge where credit belongs in another, whether the roster was loaded enough to win no matter what or if it needed the right guy to lead, and that's to say nothing of deciding whether it's more impressive to win 100 games with a good roster or 85 games with a bad one.

As a result, Manager of the Year is often treated as the award for whichever team exceeded expectations the most, usually based on results from the previous year (as we saw with Venable's White Sox going from 60 wins in 2025 to 84 this year). In other words, "Wow, he won with that roster?"

In short, there's a reason Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts has won the award just once (his inaugural season in 2016) and not for any of his MLB record-tying six 100-win seasons. The Dodgers were supposed to do that.

The Brewers, meanwhile, were never supposed to do anything like this. It has become an annual tradition for Murphy and the Brewers to grouse about preseason projections that doubt them as contenders , such as one model that had them winning 81 games this year. But as much as Murphy complains, those projections also capture why he has won Manager of the Year in every season that he has been the team's manager.

People have expected the Brewers to fade for years, given the talent they've lost. Yet this year they were better than ever, with a 103-win championship roster supported by one of the best farm systems in MLB . Odds are the wins will continue for years, and expectations should be adjusted accordingly.

articles.title: Brian Cashman Addresses Pat Murphy Ripping Yankees in Viral Video After Brewers' World Series Win
articles.summary: New York Yankees general manager Brian Cashman said he accepted Pat Murphy's apology after the Milwaukee Brewers' manager was caught on a hot mic questioning the Bronx Bombers' culture while speaking with Jake Bauers.
articles.body:
New York Yankees general manager Brian Cashman said he accepted Pat Murphy's apology after the Milwaukee Brewers' manager was caught on a hot mic questioning the Bronx Bombers' culture while speaking with Jake Bauers.

"He took the time on the greatest—within 12 hours, arguably some of the greatest times that he's had walking this planet Earth outside of the birth of his kids—to realize that he said something that he regretted, that he's caught on a live mic," Cashman told reporters Tuesday at the general managers meetings. "He wanted to take the time, track us down over here at the lowly Yankees to make sure he would apologize for that, so that meant a lot to me."

After Bauers gifted Murphy with the baseball from the final out of the team's World Series-clinching win, the manager told the first baseman—who is a free agent this winter—that he was about to be "a rich f--ker" and to "just remember when you are on that horses--t [New York] Yankees team and you guys are all playing for yourselves? Just remember, say, 'This is the way we used to do it.'"

Murphy later clarified his remarks and said he reached out to Cashman to apologize.

"I tried to explain that I wasn't talking about the 2026 Yankees," he said during an appearance on the New York Post's "The Show" podcast last week. "I was just referring to the teams with a lot of money that sign a lot of players that sometimes end up not being that 'Little Engine that Could,' so to speak—more of a high expectation, 'I gotta get mine.' I regret saying it."

For Cashman and the Yankees it's water under the bridge, though New Yorkers are certainly hoping the Bronx Bombers pony up for some upgrades in free agency this winter.

articles.title: William Contreras, Bryan Woo and 8 Other Surprise MLB Trade Candidates
articles.summary: Even with MLB insiders reporting the latest rumblings and roster construction pointing to obvious trade candidates, there is still plenty of room for a trade market surprise.
articles.body:
Even with MLB insiders reporting the latest rumblings and roster construction pointing to obvious trade candidates, there is still plenty of room for a trade market surprise.

To that point, just a few short months ago, the most obvious trade chip in baseball was dealt when Tarik Skubal joined the Los Angeles Dodgers. At the same time, few expected Adley Rutschman to be wearing a Boston Red Sox uniform in August.

Turning our attention to the 2026-27 MLB offseason, which figures to be a weird one given the upcoming CBA negotiations and expected lockout, we've highlighted 10 speculative trade candidates outside of the frequently mentioned names.

They won't all find new homes this winter, but don't be surprised if a few guys from this list end up at the center of a major winter deal.

Stats: 65 G, 41 SV, 1.44 ERA, 0.91 WHIP, 63 K, 62.1 IP, 2.9 WAR Contract: Arbitration-eligible through 2028

One of the biggest breakout stars of the 2026 season, Bryan Baker led the majors with 41 saves and helped pitch the Rays to the World Series as a reliable anchor at the back of their bullpen.

That performance, coupled with his two remaining years of club control, would make him untouchable for most teams with an eye on contending during the upcoming season. The Rays are not most teams.

With a $4.1 million projected arbitration salary, he stands to be one of the highest-paid players on the Tampa Bay roster.

For a team that is willing to get creative in deploying a bullpen, that might be incentive enough to sell high and maximize the prospect return.

Stats: 33 GS, 7-15, 4.36 ERA, 1.22 WHIP, 148 K, 188.0 IP, 1.8 WAR Contract: $39 million owed for 2027-29

With a 3.82 ERA and 108 ERA+ in 686 innings over the past four seasons, Tanner Bibee has developed into a rock-solid piece of the Guardians starting rotation.

The club signed him to a five-year, $48 million extension prior to the 2025 season, at which point he was the de facto ace of a young starting rotation.

However, since that deal was signed, Gavin Williams and Parker Messick have emerged as the present and future of the Cleveland rotation, and Bibee was relegated to one relief appearance in Game 4 of the ALDS across Cleveland's 11 playoff games.

For a Guardians team that ranked dead last in team payroll in 2026, his $7.4 million salary for the upcoming season might be reason enough to move him. Elsewhere, that would represent a team-friendly salary for even middle-of-the-rotation production.

Stats: 110 OPS+, .277/.359/.405, 29 XBH (11 HR), 21 SB, 3.4 WAR

Contract: Pre-arbitration, controllable through 2032

The Athletics have an abundance of outfield talent and a glaring need for starting pitching, and that has made controllable center fielder Denzel Clarke a popular speculative trade candidate.

However, if they hope to bring back a true impact arm in a trade, Henry Bolte would make a far more compelling centerpiece in a blockbuster deal.

His terrific offensive production made him the team's primary leadoff hitter for much of the year, while his standout defense ( 5 DRS, 5 OAA ) further boosted his value.

Clarke might be the most logical trade chip, but Bolte is the piece that could bring back a bona fide rotation anchor from a team looking for a long-term answer in center field.

Stats: 108 OPS+, .270/.341/.417, 46 XBH (18 HR), 2.9 WAR

Most teams would not entertain trading the reigning World Series MVP, but the Brewers have a well-established history of moving stars before their final season of club control.

Corbin Burnes, Devin Williams and Freddy Peralta were all dealt under those circumstances in recent years, and Milwaukee went on to win the NL Central after each trade.

If the Brewers don't see a clear path to signing an upcoming free agent long-term, they maximize his value during the offseason rather than waiting to move him when he is a trade deadline rental.

There are sticking points to this hypothetical. The potential of an extended lockout has made some teams wary of trading for upcoming free agents, and the Brewers don't have a clear in-house replacement unless they trust Bo Naylor or Jeferson Quero.

Still, recent history tells us a Contreras trade is at least a consideration in the Milwaukee front office.

Stats: 116 OPS+, .285/.313/.459, 31 XBH (14 HR), 1.7 WAR Contract: Arbitration-eligible through 2028

Over four full seasons in the big leagues, Yainer Diaz has hit .280/.307/.455 for a 112 OPS+ while averaging 30 doubles, 24 home runs and 84 RBI per 162 games played.

There is little question he is a bat-first catcher, but he did throw out 23.5 percent of base stealers in 2026, a tick above the league-average mark. He might not win a Gold Glove, but he's a capable starting backstop.

The Astros are at a crossroads and might benefit from retooling the roster, and while shortstop Jeremy Pena and third baseman Isaac Paredes are their most frequently mentioned trade chips, both could see their value undercut by a potential lockout and their looming free agency after the 2027 season.

A Diaz trade would likely be accompanied by an outside addition to fill the catcher position, but a short-term bridge to top prospects Jason Schiavone and Walker Janek might be all they need.

Stats: 86 OPS+, .227/.287/.380, 40 XBH (15 HR), 16 SB, 0.9 WAR Contract: Arbitration-eligible through 2028

Royce Lewis has shown flashes of delivering on the potential that made him the No. 1 overall pick in the 2017 draft, including a 2023 campaign where he logged a 149 OPS+ with 22 extra-base hits in 58 games.

The oft-injured former top prospect set career highs in games played (125) and plate appearances (509) last season, but his offensive production plummeted and he spent time back in Triple-A early in the year.

With an 85 OPS+ in 912 plate appearances over the last two seasons, he no longer profiles as a star-caliber player who just needs to stay healthy, but there's still a case to be made he would benefit from a change of scenery.

His $5.1 million projected arbitration figure is enough to at least mention him as a potential non-tender candidate, but at 27 years old, there is still enough untapped potential that the Twins should be able to find a trade partner if they are ready to cut ties.

SP Carmen Mlodzinski, Pittsburgh Pirates

Stats: 37 G, 12 GS, 3.95 ERA, 1.37 WHIP, 97 K, 123.0 IP, 1.3 WAR

Contract: Arbitration-eligible through 2029

Carmen Mlodzinski began last season in the Pittsburgh rotation, but he was moved to the bullpen when Jared Jones returned from the injured list in May.

He was initially placed on the restricted list after he informed the team he was not ready to pitch out of the bullpen, but that lasted one day and he ultimately embraced the role for the remainder of the season.

Mlodzinski was much better as a reliever (25 G, 2.55 ERA, 1.09 WHIP, 70.2 IP) than as a starter (12 GS, 5.85 ERA, 1.76 WHIP, 52.1 IP), but that doesn't mean he no longer prefers starting.

The Pirates did well to flip an under-the-radar controllable arm in Mike Burrows to the Astros last offseason in a three-team deal that brought back Brandon Lowe and Mason Montgomery from the Rays, and they could take a similar approach with Mlodzinski this winter.

1B Vinnie Pasquantino, Kansas City Royals

Stats: 113 OPS+, .249/.333/.428, 39 XBH (17 HR), 2.5 WAR Contract: Arbitration-eligible through 2028

From a clubhouse leadership standpoint, trading Vinnie Pasquantino might be a non-starter for the Royals, but if they are open to moving him, it makes a lot of sense in terms of roster construction.

Jac Caglianone is a first baseman miscast as a right fielder, and the defensive metrics (-4 DRS, -9 OAA) back that up, while Salvador Perez is spending more time at designated hitter and first base and less time as a catcher at this stage of his career.

Moving Pasquantino to potentially address another area of need would clear up that defensive logjam, and despite a down year by his standards, the "Pasquatch" is still a viable middle-of-the-order bat.

He is just a year removed from posting a 118 OPS+ with 33 doubles, 32 home runs and 113 RBI, and in a thin market for impact bats, his two remaining years of club control should carry significant value.

IF/OF Casey Schmitt, San Francisco Giants

Stats: 119 OPS+, .271/.301/.483, 39 XBH (21 HR), 1.5 WAR

Do the Giants think Casey Schmitt is a viable option as the everyday second baseman next season?

The 27-year-old has played 737 career innings at second base, but just 51 innings in 2026, and his middling career defensive metrics (-4 DRS, -3 OAA) suggest he might be stretched at the position on an everyday basis.

He fits best at an infield corner, but with Rafael Devers and Matt Chapman signed long-term and Bryce Eldridge absorbing the bulk of the DH at-bats, that's not going to happen. He has also played some left field (-4 DRS, -2 OAA), but is more of a stopgap there than a regular starter.

That lack of a clear defensive home could make him a trade chip as the front office looks to bolster the starting rotation behind Logan Webb, Landen Roupp and Adrian Houser this winter.

Stats: 30 GS, 4.01 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, 175 K, 173.0 IP, 2.0 WAR Contract: Arbitration-eligible through 2029

The Mariners already flipped one of their starting pitchers when they traded Luis Castillo to the White Sox at the deadline, but the rise of 2025 first-round pick Kade Anderson and emergence of Emerson Hancock still make the starting staff an area of depth.

As it stands, those two would join Logan Gilbert, George Kirby, Bryan Woo and Bryce Miller in a potential six-man rotation, with Gilbert and Kirby the most frequently mentioned trade candidates due to their proximity to free agency.

However, if the Mariners are truly looking to make a splash, Woo would undoubtedly net the most significant return.

The 26-year-old has three years of control remaining, compared to one for Gilbert and two for Kirby, and even with an uptick in his ERA last season his 3.24 FIP and underlying metrics still paint him as arguably the best pitcher on the staff.

articles.title: Ranking Braves RP Raisel Iglesias' Top 5 Landing Spots Ahead of MLB Free Agency
articles.summary: Since the beginning of 2023, current free agent closer Raisel Iglesias has recorded an MLB-best 130 saves, doing so with a 2.60 ERA.
articles.body:
Since the beginning of 2023, current free agent closer Raisel Iglesias has recorded an MLB-best 130 saves , doing so with a 2.60 ERA.

Through the first couple months of last season, it looked like his window as an elite closer had...well...closed. But he once again has been one of the best in the business over the past 16 months.

He also turns 37 in January, which could be a frightening proposition for prospective buyers.

Because while Aroldis Chapman has enjoyed quite the renaissance in his age-37 and age-38 campaigns in Boston, he and Mariano Rivera are two of the few exceptions who managed to keep Father Time at bay. Chapman has shown that relievers can remain effective into their late 30s, but Iglesias' age still represents a risk for prospective buyers.

Throw in the fact that guys like Louis Varland, Jacob Latz and Bryan Baker became All-Star closers out of nowhere this season and teams may be reluctant to invest eight figures in an aging closer.

Counterpoint: Imagine how differently things might have gone this season for the Washington Nationals and Detroit Tigers if those bullpens hadn't blown save after save after save.

With that in mind, let's take an early look at Iglesias' best/likeliest landing spots in free agency.

Already Have Their 2027 Closer, But Never Say Never

There were 13 closers who recorded at least 26 saves this season, 11 of whom are under contract through at least next year.

In alphabetical order by team, they are:

Of that bunch, the worst seasons belonged to O'Brien and Muñoz. But St. Louis arguably isn't in a "give a closer a two-year, $30M contract" sort of place in its trajectory right now, and Seattle also has virtually its entire bullpen returning in 2027, including Seranthony Domínguez, Jose A. Ferrer and Matt Brash as viable backup plans if they're worried Muñoz might be unable to reel it back in.

Rather, if anyone in that group is going to pony up eight figures for Iglesias, it's probably the Blue Jays. They have deep pockets, a considerable amount of money coming off the books this winter and a bullpen that (aside from Varland and Tyler Rogers) left much to be desired. They might also want some security in case Varland—who had a 4.66 career ERA and zero saves prior to this season—loses his mojo.

However, it's more likely that they'll focus their spending on another starting pitcher, as well as someone who can homer after the power outage (aside from Kazuma Okamoto) that they experienced this season. And if they do invest in a reliever, my guess is it'll be southpaw Adrián Morejón as opposed to Iglesias.

Beyond those 11 teams, the Los Angeles Dodgers still have Tanner Scott and Edwin Diaz, the Minnesota Twins have both Yoendrys Gómez and Jeff Hoffman for at least another year, the Baltimore Orioles just got Félix Bautista back in the final week of the regular season and the Detroit Tigers could've just brought back Kenley Jansen on a club option if they wanted a well-seasoned closer.

That's 15 teams we can probably cross off right away.

Could Use a Closer, But Have More Pressing Needs

Athletics : The A's need basically an entire pitching staff, and Hogan Harris was quietly solid after becoming the primary closer in late July. What's more, over the past two seasons, Iglesias has a ground ball rate of just 33.8 percent, which could be a disaster at Sutter Health Park.

Cincinnati Reds : Following Emilio Pagán declining his $10M player option for next season, maybe the Reds consider Iglesias. But they've already lost Hunter Greene to Tommy John surgery and had what would have been the worst pitching staff in 2026 were it not for Chase Burns. Throw in the lack of bats outside of Elly De La Cruz and Sal Stewart—not to mention a history of being frugal—and it's simply not a likely/good fit.

Colorado Rockies : We decided to at least mention all 30 teams, but the Rockies have suffered at least 100 losses in four consecutive seasons and let's just say a closer isn't the band-aid solution to their woes.

Kansas City Royals : The Royals had a $13M club option on Carlos Estévez if that's where they wanted to invest that type of money. But if they're spending any real money this winter, it should go toward upgrading the outfield and perhaps adding at least one more starting pitcher.

Los Angeles Angels : If he stays healthy, Ben Joyce is the plan at closer moving forward. But even if the Halos don't have faith in him, teams that have suffered 11 consecutive losing seasons probably shouldn't be spending big on closers. Plus, the last time they invested in Iglesias, they subsequently salary-dumped him to Atlanta.

San Francisco Giants : Randy Rodríguez missed all of 2026 after undergoing Tommy John surgery, but he's presumably Plan A for saves next season. The Giants also have several holes in their lineup to address and need to add multiple starting pitchers, unless they are irrationally confident in the bevy of rookies they called up late in a lost season.

Usually, when a closer is up for grabs, the team that most recently employed said closer is going to be a top five candidate to sign him. At any rate, there is now an Iglesias-sized hole in Atlanta's bullpen.

But the Braves do have Robert Suarez, who had an MLB-best 76 saves between the 2024-25 seasons in San Diego. They also have Didier Fuentes, who broke out in a big way and reasonably could be the next man up if Suarez gets injured or struggles. (He also could move into the starting rotation, though. If that's Atlanta's plan for him, re-signing Iglesias might be more likely.)

Plus, with Mauricio Dubón, Tyler Mahle and Martín Pérez also now free agents, Atlanta has bigger fish to fry than aggressively reinforcing the back of an already solid bullpen.

And after investing $13M in a closer (Pete Fairbanks) this past winter before watching him post a negative-1.3 bWAR , the Marlins—who had the lowest payroll in all of baseball in both 2025 and 2026 and can't exactly afford to whiff on eight-figure salaries—will probably be reluctant to go back down that road.

Just to play devil's advocate, though, what if they had invested in the correct closer? One who had stayed healthy and didn't post an ERA north of 6.00 while blowing four saves and suffering three other losses? That could have been a season-changer for a team that didn't miss the playoffs by all that much.

If any team is going to invest in a third closer with a $15M luxury tax salary, of course it's the New York Mets.

They already have Devin Williams signed through 2028. Kodai Senga—who went 8-for-9 in save chances while Williams was on the IL—is also signed through at least next season, and presumably not re-entering the starting rotation.

But, hey, what's one more in the grand scheme of run prevention?

We're being a bit facetious there, but for as underwhelming as both Williams and Senga were this season, you never know. The Mets also already traded away Luke Weaver, Huascar Brazobán, Brooks Raley and AJ Minter and enter the offseason with a less than enviable bullpen situation as a whole.

Pittsburgh's closer situation was a mess for the first half of the season, but they appear to have found something special in Mason Montgomery, who had a 1.22 ERA over his final 38 appearances, going 18-for-19 in save chances.

However, Montgomery had a 5.01 ERA over the previous two seasons in Tampa Bay, as well as a 4.83 ERA through his first 32 appearances of 2026. And banking on saves from Dennis Santana—who had a breakthrough year in 2025 after posting a 4.76 ERA through his first seven seasons in the majors—is how they ended up in a pickle at closer this year.

If they're willing to repeat last winter's spending spree (by their historical standards) with a few more Ryan O'Hearn ($14.5M AAV) and Marcell Ozuna ($12M AAV) types of deals, maybe Iglesias could be a prime target for them. Though, figuring out how to replace Brandon Lowe's bat (if he declines his qualifying offer) should be their main focus.

The big question here is how much faith the Snakes have in Justin Martínez.

The 25-year-old flamethrower is signed through at least 2029 and returned from Tommy John surgery in mid-August, pitching quite well over the final six weeks of the regular season. However, they almost exclusively used him in low-leverage situations, even though their closer situation was a five-headed committee.

Most likely, the plan is to have Martínez back in the closer saddle whenever the 2027 season begins. But this bullpen has been gutted by free agency, set to return just two of the seven pitchers who appeared in at least 40 games this season (Brandyn Garcia and Juan Morillo).

Could this be the year that they pony up for a closer for a change?

Giving Mark Melancon a two-year, $14M contract five years ago was the biggest investment Arizona has ever made in a relief pitcher, which is a bit self-evident from the revolving door they've had in the ninth inning since J.J. Putz was their go-to guy back in 2011-12.

Also, save for Joe Mantiply (who has saved three games in his MLB career) randomly serving as Arizona's representative in 2022, this team hasn't had a reliever named an All-Star since José Valverde in 2007.

After narrowly missing the postseason in both 2024 and 2026, the appetite for a real closer might be at an all-time high in the desert.

The Yankees would rank No. 1 on this list if the question were simply: Is the team likely to invest in a closer this offseason?

That's because right alongside Iglesias atop the list of free-agent closers is David Bednar, who has a 2.39 ERA and 45 saves since going from Pittsburgh to New York ahead of the 2025 trade deadline.

The Bronx Bombers also lost Ryan Yarbrough, Tim Hill, Paul Blackburn and John Schreiber to free agency. They already dumped Camilo Doval in August. And Fernando Cruz is trying to rehab from a partial UCL tear without undergoing surgery. If he is unsuccessful, though, the Yankees are going to need to either replace or re-sign every single pitcher who tallied a save for them this season.

They do at least have Brent Headrick coming back after leading the team with 29 holds, but it's hard to imagine he becomes the closer.

The options appear to be A) bringing back Bednar, B) bringing in Iglesias or C) maybe trading with the Dodgers if they can get Edwin Díaz on the cheap.

How much is Bednar going to cost, though?

Coincidentally, Iglesias is the perfect comp.

Bednar will be 32 years old when next season begins. He has 146 career saves and a 3.03 ERA.

Heading into 2022, Iglesias was 32 with 140 career saves and a 3.06 ERA. After turning down a qualifying offer (which Bednar also figures to do in a few weeks' time), Iglesias got a four-year, $58M contract from the Angels. Adjusting for inflation, that's probably more like a four-year, $66M deal now.

Though Bednar has been solid for the Yankees, a shorter-term deal with Iglesias might be preferable.

This past January—when the White Sox were fresh off their third consecutive season of at least 100 losses and didn't feel like a remotely legitimate threat to reach the postseason—they signed Seranthony Domínguez to a two-year, $20M contract.

They subsequently traded him away for Luis Castillo, but if they were willing to spend like that for a semi-established closer before turning the proverbial corner, why wouldn't they also do so for a much more established closer now that there are routinely leads that need protecting?

Grant Taylor fared pretty well as Chicago's primary source of saves from July 4 onward, but he was a far cry from "lock him in as our main guy in 2027" dominant. He also pitched multiple innings in 31 of his 60 appearances and only started getting save chances because no one else was taking up the mantle.

In other words, bringing in a guy like Iglesias while letting Taylor and Bryan Hudson share the set-up duties could be the answer for a bullpen that sure was running on fumes toward the end of the regular season.

At any rate, after leading the AL in scoring, the White Sox don't need to worry about spending on bats this winter. If 2024 No. 5 overall pick Hagen Smith—who was spectacular in relief over the final two months—can make a seamless transition into the starting rotation alongside Sean Burke and Davis Martin, they shouldn't need to get too aggressive about upgrading the rotation. And they can definitely afford to do some spending this winter.

After half a decade of haplessly rebuilding, the Nationals finally showed legitimate signs of life in 2026. In addition to having one of the highest-scoring offenses, Cade Cavalli emerged as the ace-caliber arm they have been desperately lacking since trading away Max Scherzer in 2021.

Sweet sassy molassy was this a horrendous bullpen, though, with fixing the closer situation offering a more obvious opportunity for improvement than anywhere else in baseball.

The Nationals obliterated the MLB record for blown saves in a season, ending up with 42.

While not all of their blown saves resulted in losses, posting a 6.39 ERA between the eighth and ninth innings is unquestionably the reason Washington was unable to snap its streak of losing seasons.

Sixteen different pitchers tallied at least one save, but 13 Nationals pitchers blew multiple saves. Meanwhile, their only pitcher with at least seven successful saves was Clayton Beeter, who went 12-for-19 before closing out the season in Triple-A Rochester.

And they are certainly familiar with Iglesias' work. Since landing with Atlanta in 2022, he has a 0.90 ERA against the Nationals, going 11-for-12 in save chances. That's a level of consistency in the ninth inning that Washington hasn't had on its side since Chad Cordero in 2005.

They do also need to make some additions to the starting rotation if they're legitimately going for it in 2027, but they have nothing but room in the budget to address multiple problem areas.

CJ Abrams' salary ($4.2M in 2026) is surely going to spike in arbitration, but James Wood still has one more preposterously underpaid year of pre-arbitration remaining. And no one else is earmarked for more than $5M in 2027.

This is the window back to relevance, if they want it. And landing a legitimate closer is a non-negotiable step in that journey.

With starting pitchers Kevin Gausman, Shota Imanaga, Matthew Boyd, David Peterson and Clay Holmes all now free agents—not to mention lineup regulars Ian Happ, Seiya Suzuki, Carson Kelly and Michael Conforto—get ready for the Chicago Cubs to feature prominently in a lot of landing-spots articles this winter.

But with the adventures they had in their bullpen this season, making a serious splash at closer has to be near the top of their to-do list.

Granted, if Daniel Palencia had been able to stay healthy, maybe the situation wouldn't have gotten so problematic, as the 2025 team leader in saves did have three within his first nine appearances this season. But by the time he landed on the IL for the second time in mid-June, Chicago was already looking at 10 saves and 10 blown saves for the year.

In the end, Jacob Webb led the team in saves (nine), holds (nine) and blown saves (eight), which is a rather bizarre triple crown of sorts.

The only particularly reliable or durable closer they've had in the past nine years was Craig Kimbrel in 2021—and he was a disaster in both 2019 and 2020 before rebounding and being traded to the White Sox for Nick Madrigal and Codi Heuer.

It's time to change that narrative by actually investing in a closer for a change.

Because despite the aforementioned free agents, the Cubs are still very much in a championship window.

Pete Crow-Armstrong, Alex Bregman, Dansby Swanson, Nico Hoerner and Michael Busch aren't going anywhere any time soon. Justin Steele should(?) be back for Opening Day, with Cade Horton joining him at some point mid-season. Maybe Edward Cabrera bounces back in a big way, too, while Ben Brown picks up where he left off before his neck injury.

Something needs to be done about the ninth inning, though, and Iglesias should be the answer.

articles.title: MLB MVP 2026 Final Odds and Predictions for AL and NL Awards
articles.summary: The voters have spoken.
articles.body:
Or they're in the process of speaking, rather.

MLB award season is officially upon us, and some coveted hardware has already been handed out. Kevin McGonigle of the Detroit Tigers and Sal Stewart of the Cincinnati Reds claimed Rookie of the Year honors in their respective leagues, while the Chicago White Sox's Will Venable and Pat Murphy of the World Series champion Milwaukee Brewers were named Managers of the Year.

Hats off to the winners so far, but there are still some huge honors to be handed out. The Cy Youngs will be crowned Wednesday night in fact, and then the MVPs will get their turn under the spotlight on Thursday.

These races might lack suspense—more on that in a minute—but let's examine why the favorites are regarded as such and see whether any surprises are in store. With FanDuel having pulled its odds for these awards, we'll use their end-of-season odds from September 19 (h/t Fox Sports ).

Cam Schlittler, RHP, New York Yankees -50000 (bet $50,000 to win $100)

Dylan Cease, RHP, Toronto Blue Jays +3300 (bet $100 to win $3,300)

Parker Messick, LHP, Cleveland Guardians

Jacob Misiorowski, RHP, Milwaukee Brewers -20000

Cristopher Sánchez, LHP, Philadelphia Phillies

Yordan Alvarez, DH, Houston Astros -20000

Junior Caminero, 3B, Tampa Bay Rays +1200

Pete Crow-Armstrong, CF, Chicago Cubs -1500

Shohei Ohtani, SP/DH, Los Angeles Dodgers +750

There isn't a heavier favorite in the field than Schlittler for AL Cy Young. And that's pretty remarkable given the kind of campaigns just authored by Cease (2.40 ERA with 239 strikeouts in 169 innings) and Messick (2.56 ERA and a 1.06 WHIP across 186.1 innings).

Those players were dominant; Schlittler was otherworldly. He had an AL-leading 1.95 ERA, a none-shall-pass 0.919 WHIP and 239 strikeouts against 49 walks in 193.2 innings. He'll turn overwhelming favorite to runaway winner here shortly.

It's a similar story in the MVP race. Caminero crushed it (42 homers, 101 RBI, 100 runs scored), and Witt was good-to-great in all facets (18 homers, 45 steals, 94 runs and lockdown defense), but Alvarez had the top tier all to himself.

A slugger by trade with the power production to back it up (42 homers, 106 RBI), Alvarez was also this season's best hitte r overall. He paced the entire Majors with a .316 average, and he held down the same No. 1 spot—by comfortable margins—in on-base percentage (.432), slugging percentage (.601) and OPS (1.033).

It's kind of comical to think Misiorowski isn't the strongest favorite among award finalists. Not to take anything away from Sale (2.16 ERA, 11.1 K/9) or Sánchez (18 wins, 2.91 ERA and 231 strikeouts in 207 innings), as each was awesome in his own right.

But Misiorowski and his historic heat might have been the best show in baseball this season. He led the Majors in...well, everything basically: ERA (1.80), strikeouts (252), strikeout rate (37.9 percent) and WHIP (0.80). As MLB.com relayed, Misirowski posted the lowest opponents' average on record for a full season (.157).

If there's a "close" race in this field, by default it has to be the NL MVP. And that's essentially only (relatively) close because of Ohtani's unique two-way talents, which have helped him capture MVP honors in four of the past five seasons (two in each league).

But injuries bothered Ohtani this season, and he wasn't his typical self. He was still ridiculous (30 homers, 170 combined runs and RBI in 135 games; 8-2 with a 1.79 ERA and 95 strikeouts over 85.2 innings pitched), but not quite as productive as he had been. Turang was great, too, pairing Gold Glove defense with 21 homers, 19 steals 202 combined runs and RBI.

Still, neither really measured up to Crow-Armstrong, who was brilliant both at the plate and on the field. He joined the 40/40 club (45 homers, 41 steals), led the Majors with 119 runs, tallied the fourth-most RBI (107) and paced the NL in slugging percentage (.570) and OPS (.943). If that wasn't enough, Crow-Armstrong also earned the NL's Platinum Glove award. He'll soon add MVP to his list of accolades.

articles.title: New MLB Trade Rumors Reveal Dylan Crews Buzz, Nationals' Asking Price in Potential Deal
articles.summary: Having failed to live up to his potential thus far in his career, the Washington Nationals are open to trading former No. 2 overall pick Dylan Crews this offseason.
articles.body:
Having failed to live up to his potential thus far in his career, the Washington Nationals are open to trading former No. 2 overall pick Dylan Crews this offseason.

Per The Athletic's Spencer Nussbaum , Crews has been a popular name bantered about at the GM meetings and the Nationals "won't take" him off the table as they have other players on the roster.

As for what the Nationals would want in a deal for Crews, Nussbaum cited multiple teams that have indicated they are in search of "controllable starting pitching."

Crews was the top position player prospect in the 2023 draft and was taken one pick after Paul Skenes was selected by the Pittsburgh Pirates. He was regarded by most analysts as the best player in the class leading up to the draft after a stellar three-year run at LSU.

MLB.com's Prospect Pipeline praised Crews' "plus-plus" hit tool and plus power that allowed him to control the zone and make consistently strong contact. He hit

Crews started the 2024 season as the No. 8 overall prospect in MLB. He was called up by the Nationals in August of that season and was expected to be a staple in their outfield.

Things haven't translated for Crews thus far with a .217/.285/.363 slash line in 897 plate appearances over the past three seasons. He missed time due to injuries in 2025 and started 2026 in Triple-A before being recalled on May 19.

Crews will turn 25 on Feb. 26 and is under team control through the 2031 season, so it's easy to understand why opposing clubs would have interest in adding him.

The Nationals have a crowded outfield mix with James Wood under team control through 2030 and Jacob Young agreeing to a four-year contract extension last week that will keep him as their starting centerfielder.

Daylen Lile wasn't great at the plate in 2026 after a strong 91-game performance the previous year, but he showed more power with 22 homers in 160 games than Crews has in his MLB career thus far.

Starting pitching is a necessity for the Nationals if they want to be a playoff contender in 2027. Their rotation ranked 20th in ERA and 29th in innings pitched last season.

There aren't many teams eager to give up starters with years of team control, but a club that has a strong surplus in the rotation and is looking for a potential boost in the outfield could make a compelling offer to the Nationals for Crews.

articles.title: New Yankees Rumors on Alec Bohm Interest in 2026 MLB Free Agency After Ryan McMahon's Struggles
articles.summary: The New York Yankees are reportedly seeking an upgrade over third baseman Ryan McMahon following his disappointing 2026 season.
articles.body:
The New York Yankees are reportedly seeking an upgrade over third baseman Ryan McMahon following his disappointing 2026 season.

Jon Heyman of the New York Post reported that the Yankees "are looking closely at" free-agent third baseman Alec Bohm. New York's interest comes after McMahon hit just .213 with 11 home runs and 41 RBI in 124 regular-season games, with his average dropping to .143 in the playoffs.

A seven-year veteran who has spent his entire career with the Philadelphia Phillies, Bohm hit .249 with 15 homers and 88 RBI in 155 games. While those numbers may not jump off the page, Heyman noted that he "performed very well after a brutal April."

The Yankees went 93-68 and lost in the ALDS for the second straight season, extending their World Series title drought that dates back to 2009. Heyman reported that they have "prioritized the infield" in free agency after McMahon "struggled so badly at the plate last year and also prefer a right-handed bat, so Bohm is a potential fit."

In addition to replacing McMahon, the Yankees will also have to address the middle of their infield after allowing second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. to become an unrestricted free agent .

Still, it's been quite some time since the Bronx Bombers have been big spenders in free agency, so it doesn't sound like New York is on the verge of any splashy moves. Heyman noted that Bohm "would likely be looking at a relatively short deal," so it can be expected that the Yankees will be trying to improve around the margins this winter.

articles.title: Brad Ausmus Named Astros Manager, Agrees to Contract to Replace Joe Espada
articles.summary: The Houston Astros hired former All-Star catcher Brad Ausmus, who has spent the last three seasons as a bench coach for the New York Yankees, as their next manager on Wednesday.
articles.body:
The Houston Astros hired former All-Star catcher Brad Ausmus, who has spent the last three seasons as a bench coach for the New York Yankees, as their next manager on Wednesday.

Ausmus' appointment comes two weeks after the Astros named Randy Flores their new general manager.

The Astros needed a new manager after parting ways with ex-manager, Joe Espada, after the expiration of his three-year contract.

Last year, Houston went 81-81, but that was good enough to win an AL West that featured four other teams with losing records.

However, the Chicago White Sox swept the host Astros two games to zero in the American League Wild Card Round, outscoring them 13-6.

Houston dealt with an assortment of injuries, including ones to catcher Yainer Diaz, shortstop Jeremy Peña and second baseman Jose Altuve. The pitching staff was hit hard by injuries, with 19 different players starting at least one game for Houston this year. Only one pitcher (Peter Lambert, 29) started more than 20 games this season.

The Astros ultimately had MLB's seventh-highest ERA (4.45). Houston scored a slightly above league-average 4.53 runs (the average was 4.48), but that was partially because superstar Yordan Alvarez had a dominant season (42 home runs, 106 RBI and an MLB-high 1.033 OPS).

Houston's gone in the wrong direction since winning the 2022 World Series. The Astros were one victory away from taking the 2023 AL pennant, but they haven't won a playoff game since. Now the Astros hope a leadership change will jump-start the team.

The 57-year-old Ausmus caught for the San Diego Padres, Detroit Tigers, Astros, and Los Angeles Dodgers over his 18-year playing career. He was with the Astros for 10 seasons (1997-1998, 2001-2008) and served as their backstop for three NL Central winners and one NL pennant (2005).

Ausmus was an All-Star in 1999 and won three Gold Gloves as well.

After his playing career ended in 2010, Ausmus became a field executive for the San Diego Padres (2011-2013) before serving as the Detroit Tigers' manager from 2014-2017. The 2014 Tigers went 90-72 and won the American League Central but lost to the Baltimore Orioles in the American League Division Series.

The Tigers slid from there, going 74-87 in 2015. They improved to 86-75 in 2016 but then tumbled to the division cellar (64-98) in 2017. Detroit did not offer him a new deal, and his four-year contract expired.

Ausmus worked as a special assistant to Los Angeles Angels general manager Billy Eppler in 2018 and then got promoted to manager in 2019, but L.A. struggled, going 72-90. The team parted ways after the season.

In 2022, Ausmus worked as the Oakland Athletics' bench coach. He turned down the opportunity to return . Ausmus connected with the Yankees and has been the team's bench coach for three seasons.

Now he's back to calling the shots on the bench as Houston hopes the return of one of the team's best catchers in team history gives the franchise the jolt it needs.

articles.title: New Tarik Skubal Rumors on Blue Jays Links amid Mets, Dodgers, Padres Buzz in MLB Free Agency
articles.summary: The MLB offseason doesn't really kick into gear until the Toronto Blue Jays launch what's likely to be a futile pursuit for one of the best free agents on the board.
articles.body:
The MLB offseason doesn't really kick into gear until the Toronto Blue Jays launch what's likely to be a futile pursuit for one of the best free agents on the board.

The New York Post 's Jon Heyman reported Wednesday the Blue Jays "are a player" for two-time Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal. They're expected to receive the opportunity to meet him directly to make their pitch.

According to Heyman, the New York Mets, Los Angeles Dodgers and San Diego Padres are also in the mix.

Toronto generally hasn't been a destination for major stars, but that's not through a lack of trying.

The franchise got deep into negotiations with Shohei Ohtani before he signed with the Dodgers. There was a serious effort made to land Juan Soto. Last year, it was the same story with Kyle Tucker.

Links to Skubal were inevitable for the Blue Jays given their recent history.

It goes without saying the southpaw would be a massive addition to the starting rotation. Dylan Cease delivered on the mound after signing a $210 million contract, and Trey Yesavage was solid in his first full MLB season. Beyond that, there are a lot of uncertainties with Max Scherzer and Shane Bieber hitting the open market.

The fanbase might have a mix of emotions with Skubal now a confirmed target. As encouraging as it is when your favorite team tries to sign marquee free agents, some will think we already know how this story will end for Toronto. It can become demoralizing after a while when an organization is perceived as always being the bridesmaid and never the bride.

As long as general manager Ross Atkins is evaluating other pitching targets, there shouldn't be too much downside to chasing Skubal.

articles.title: Astros announce hiring of franchise legend Brad Ausmus as next manager
articles.summary: Brad Ausmus is returning to the Astros.
articles.body:
The Houston Astros are turning to a familiar face to run the team in 2027. Former catcher Brad Ausmus will be the team's next manager, the team confirmed Wednesday.

In a statement, the team confirmed that Ausmus — who spent the past few seasons as the New York Yankees' bench coach — will be available to speak with reporters Friday.

Astros general manager Randy Flores said he was "thrilled" to have Ausmus back in the organization. Ausmus echoed that sentiment, saying he was "excited to be back in Houston."

Ausmus has plenty of familiarity with the organization. He spent 10 seasons with the Astros as a player, and is regarded as the best catcher in the franchise's history. Ausmus' defensive prowess and knowledge of the game made him a popular managerial candidate once he retired after the 2010 MLB season.

It didn't take long before Ausmus got his first shot at that role. After spending a few years in the San Diego Padres' front office, Ausmus was hired by the Detroit Tigers ahead of the 2014 MLB season. He spent four years with the club, compiling a 314-332 record. Ausmus reached the playoffs just one time in Detroit, though failed to win a postseason game with the team.

Following his firing, Ausmus joined the Los Angeles Angels, where he was a special assistant before being named the team's manager in 2019. The Angels went 72-90 under Ausmus, who was not brought back for a second season.

Since then, Ausmus has served as a bench coach with both the Athletics and Yankees.

The Astros were in the market for a new manager after parting ways with Joe Espada in October. Espada posted a .528 winning percentage in three seasons as the team's manager, but failed to lead the Astros to postseason success.

In addition to Ausmus, the team reportedly spoke with former St. Louis Cardinals legend Albert Pujols and Texas Rangers bench coach Luis Urueta for the job.

Ultimately, the team went with Ausmus, who has previous experience as an MLB manager and a lot of goodwill from Astros fans.

That goodwill, however, could be tested early. While the Espada era ended in disappointment, he did lead the team to two playoff appearances in three seasons.

If that wasn't good enough for the Astros, expectations will likely be even higher for Ausmus in his first year with the team.

articles.title: New Phillies Rumors on Randy Arozarena, Teruaki Sato, Seiya Suzuki Interest in MLB Free Agency
articles.summary: The Philadelphia Phillies have identified the outfield as a major priority in free agency.
articles.body:
The Philadelphia Phillies have identified the outfield as a major priority in free agency.

The Athletic's Matt Gelb reported Wednesday that Philadelphia has "expressed interest in the biggest outfield targets" and cited Teruaki Sato, Seiya Suzuki and Randy Arozarena.

According to Gelb, the Phillies "are quite intrigued" by Sato specifically.

Sometimes, a team will play its cards close to the vest in order to throw rivals off the scent or maintain as much leverage with potential targets. Phillies president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski, on the other hand, came right out and announced one of his offseason objectives.

"I will say one thing: We have to have an outfielder," he told reporters Tuesday. "Right now, we don't have an outfielder. But is that more important than some other things? I guess it depends upon who that outfielder is."

Assuming Justin Crawford is a lock in center field, Philly has some room to upgrade in the corner slots with Brandon Marsh and Bryan De La Cruz penciled in as the starters.

Suzuki, Arozarena and Sato are second, third and fifth in Bleacher Report's free-agent rankings for the 2026/27 class.

Suzuki hit 30-plus homers in three of his first five years in MLB and owns a .269/.351/.472 career slash line. Arozarena is coming off his best full season in the bigs. He had 26 home runs, 26 stolen bases and slugged .484 with the Seattle Mariners. Sato claimed a Triple Crown after leading the Japanese Central League in average (.306), home runs (39) and RBI (106).

And while Sato is unproven in MLB, he's younger than both Suzuki (32) and Arozarena (31). He'll turn 28 next March.

The clock is ticking with the NPB standout. He and the other players coming over from Japan have to sign prior to the expiration of the current collective bargaining agreement on Dec. 2.

If the Phillies land Sato, that would likely remove them from the discussion for Suzuki and Arozarena. Should Sato go elsewhere, their pursuit of the MLB veterans would presumably intensify.

articles.title: New Tarik Skubal Rumors Update Dodgers' Stance on Contract Talks in MLB Free Agency
articles.summary: If the Los Angeles Dodgers bring back Tarik Skubal, they hope to do so on a deal structured similarly to the one they gave Kyle Tucker last offseason.
articles.body:
If the Los Angeles Dodgers bring back Tarik Skubal, they hope to do so on a deal structured similarly to the one they gave Kyle Tucker last offseason.

Per The Athletic's Katie Woo , the Dodgers are primarily interested in retaining Skubal on a short-term contract with a high average annual salary.

Tucker, arguably the best free agent available last offseason, signed a four-year, $240 million contract with LA that has opt-outs after years two and three.

The deal included $30 million in deferred money, bringing the present-day average annual value down from $60 million to $57.1 million that still set an MLB record for highest average annual salary ahead of Juan Soto's $51 million.

There are reasons to believe it might be difficult to make a short-term contract to appeal to Skubal. The first is Tucker signed his deal going into his age-29 season, so he could potentially hit the market again at 31 or 32 if he exercises his opt-out.

Skubal is going into his age-30 season and even if he were to get an opt-out after his second year, the market for a 32-year-old pitcher is not always robust.

Zack Wheeler, Framber Valdez and Jacob deGrom are currently the only pitchers making at least $30 million annually who signed their most recent contracts at the age of 32 or older.

Another potential issue for the Dodgers is Skubal is widely believed to get offers that will be the richest ever given to a pitcher by total value. Yoshinobu Yamamoto currently holds the record at $325 million over 12 years on his deal with the Dodgers.

MLB Trade Rumors predicted a nine-year, $425 million deal for Skubal.

Another factor potentially working against Skubal signing a short-term deal is he already had Tommy John surgery in college and missed time last season due to loose bodies in his elbow that required surgery.

This is Skubal's first chance to secure whatever contract he wants. His injury history, while not extensive, might lead him to take the biggest deal.

Of course, it's entirely reasonable to think Skubal enjoyed his time with the Dodgers and their history of spending to improve the roster would appeal to him that he would accept a short-term offer.

Skubal posted a 2.61 ERA with 70 strikeouts over 62 innings in 10 starts with the Dodgers after being acquired in a trade with the Detroit Tigers. He also allowed three earned runs and struck out 14 over 11 innings in two playoff starts.

articles.title: New Dodgers Rumors on Teoscar Hernandez Trade, Mookie Betts, Josue De Paula's Role
articles.summary: The Los Angeles Dodgers have "pause" regarding a potential trade of outfielder Teoscar Hernández to free up a spot for 21-year-old outfield prospect Josue de Paula, per Katie Woo of The Athletic, who reported the news and provided more context on that front on Wednesday.
articles.body:
The Los Angeles Dodgers have "pause" regarding a potential trade of outfielder Teoscar Hernández to free up a spot for 21-year-old outfield prospect Josue de Paula, per Katie Woo of The Athletic, who reported the news and provided more context on that front on Wednesday.

"The Dodgers rostered the oldest position-playing group in baseball last season, and they want to get younger. An obvious way to do that is to deal Teoscar Hernández, whom the Dodgers shopped last winter, to clear a spot for De Paula. But because a pending lockout will prohibit clubs from contacting players on their 40-man roster, there will be no way for the organization to assess De Paula's development throughout the offseason. Per a team source, that has given the Dodgers pause about whether they should trade Hernández."

Woo also reported that the Dodgers are keeping Mookie Betts at shortstop.

"The organization has no plans to move Betts from shortstop and is not interested in a blockbuster trade for a younger player at the position, despite much speculation. Instead, they remain focused on adding to their depth and keeping their core intact."

The plan there, Woo reported, is for the Dodgers to find a "stopgap option who can play second base and shortstop." Essentially, L.A. is reportedly looking for a "right-handed middle infielder" a la Miguel Rojas, who retired after last season.

The 34-year-old Hernández has played his last three seasons with the Dodgers, helping the team win the 2024 and 2025 World Series and playing key roles each time. The 11-year veteran's best season in town was 2024, when he hit .272 (.840 OPS) with 33 home runs and 99 RBI.

Hernández hasn't fared as well since, and he's dealt with numerous injuries. Of note, he missed a month in 2026 with a Grade 1 left hamstring strain. Still, Hernández is productive and wielded an above-average bat, hitting .267 (.759 OPS) with 16 homers and 64 RBI in 125 games last season.

Hernández is under contract next year ($22.2 million). L.A. has a team option in 2028 and can part ways with a $6.5 million buyout.

We'll see what the Dodgers decide there down the road, with the caveat that a lockout (the current collective bargaining agreement expires on Dec. 1) would put a stop to any deal, as MLB teams can't trade players or sign free agents during that span.

As for De Paula, he's the future in town. MLB.com has him as the No. 4 prospect in the majors. The 6'3", 185-pound prospect has a lofty MLB.com scouting report drawing comparisons to presumptive American League MVP and Houston Astros superstar Yordan Alvarez.

"De Paula draws comparisons to a slightly smaller but more athletic version of Yordan Alvarez, thanks to his precocious combination of swing decisions and exit velocities," the report reads.

De Paula played 11 MLB games last season, hitting .323 (1.081 OPS) with a homer and seven RBI. He crushed Double-A pitching in 2026, hitting .303 (.948 OPS) with 27 homers and 104 RBI in 124 games. He'll be playing in L.A. full time before too long.

There's no question on Betts' status as shortstop. The four-time World Series winner and eight-time All-Star had a rough start to the season, hitting .181 (.591 OPS) through June 12. However, Betts turned things around in short order, hitting .288 (.856 OPS) with 17 home runs and 52 RBI in his final 88 regular-season games.

The Dodgers do need a replacement for Rojas, who played 446 games over his final four seasons with L.A., primarily in the middle infield. Rojas played a crucial role for the team and will forever be a World Series hero after his game-tying homer in Game 7 of the 2025 Fall Classic.

In the meantime, the general manager meetings continue in Las Vegas, but the clock ticks toward a potential lockout in December.

articles.title: Everything Scott Boras Said About Tarik Skubal Amid Dodgers, Mets Rumors in MLB Free Agency
articles.summary: Free agency is officially here in MLB because super-agent Scott Boras went on the record to discuss one of his top clients in a way only he can.
articles.body:
Free agency is officially here in MLB because super-agent Scott Boras went on the record to discuss one of his top clients in a way only he can .

Boras is the agent for two-time Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal, by far the top player on the market. Speaking with reporters Wednesday, he described "a dominant and strong Sku-bull market" and said "there is only one Tarik card."

Boras added that interested suitors are "ready for the Skubal dive."

The expiration of the current collective bargaining agreement at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1 is looming over the entire sport, and it will inevitably impact some free agents. Boras suggested it's still business as usual in some cases.

ESPN's Jeff Passan reported earlier this month that Skubal is expected to sign prior to the CBA deadline.

According to the Associated Press' Ronald Blum , six teams are in the running but only three were confirmed: New York Mets, Los Angeles Dodgers and San Diego Padres. Jon Heyman of the New York Post then identified the Toronto Blue Jays as a contender.

There's some risk in signing Skubal to the kind of contract he's in line to earn when so much about MLB's financial outlook in 2027 and beyond is murky. League owners have proposed dramatic measures such as a hard salary cap and a maximum length on contracts to free agents.

ESPN's Kiley McDaniel projected Skubal will get $352 million over eight years, while The Athletic's Tim Britton went a little higher (nine years, $405 million). Spending $40-plus million on a starting pitcher is a sizable cost on its own. Now imagine doing that with an even more restrictive cap structure in place.

Still, the opportunity to land Skubal might be too good for a playoff contender to pass up before free agency potentially grounds to a halt.

articles.title: MLB Cy Young and All-MLB Team Awards Show, Latest Rumors, Updates and Reaction
articles.summary: It is MLB awards week as we slap a bow on the 2026 season, and on Wednesday night the AL and NL Cy Young winners and All-MLB team selections will be revealed.
articles.body:
It is MLB awards week as we slap a bow on the 2026 season, and on Wednesday night the AL and NL Cy Young winners and All-MLB team selections will be revealed.

This year also marks the first time the Baseball Writers' Association of America will be handing out AL and NL Reliever of the Year awards.

Then later in the evening, the MLB Awards will include the All-MLB team announcement, Comeback Player of the Year, Hank Aaron Award and other non-BBWAA hardware.

Keep it right here for all the winners, updates and live reaction on a busy Wednesday night of MLB award week.

Let's wrap up MLB Awards night with a look at the full 2026 All-MLB first team selections.

Pete Alonso - Baltimore Orioles Yordan Alvarez - Houston Astros Randy Arozarena - Seattle Mariners Junior Caminero - Tampa Bay Rays Willson Contreras - Boston Red Sox Yandy Díaz - Tampa Bay Rays Riley Greene - Detroit Tigers Ben Rice - New York Yankees Miguel Vargas - Chicago White Sox Bobby Witt Jr. - Kansas City Royals

CJ Abrams - Washington Nationals Jake Bauers - Milwaukee Brewers Pete Crow-Armstrong - Chicago Cubs Elly De La Cruz - Cincinnati Reds Shohei Ohtani - Los Angeles Dodgers Matt Olson - Atlanta Braves Kyle Schwarber - Philadelphia Phillies Sal Stewart - Cincinnati Reds Fernando Tatis Jr. - San Diego Padres Jordan Walker - St. Louis Cardinals

Winner: Pete Crow-Armstrong, Chicago Cubs

First Team: Gabriel Moreno, ARI Second Team: William Contreras, MIL

The NL batting title and his usual stellar defense was enough to make Gabriel Moreno the best all-around catcher in baseball in 2026.

First Team: Pete Alonso, BAL Second Team: Willson Contreras, BOS

Alonso was the unanimous choice in B/R's All-MLB vote, and while not much went right in Baltimore this year, he was fantastic in the first season with the club.

First Team: Mason Miller, SD First Team: Louis Varland, TOR

Second Team: Bryan Baker, TB Second Team: Cade Smith, CLE

All-MLB honors mirror the BBWAA awards, with Bryan Baker sliding in behind Louis Varland here after just being named Mariano Rivera AL Reliever of the Year.

Far too much overlap in this entire MLB awards process. Guessing overhauling awards season won't be super high on the CBA negotiating list.

Mariano Rivera and Trevor Hoffman Reliever of the Year Awards

Mariano Rivera Award (AL): Bryan Baker, TB

Trevor Hoffman Award (NL): Mason Miller, SD

Earlier tonight, the BBWAA handed out a Reliever of the Year award for the first time, and while they agreed on the Mason Miller selection, it was Blue Jays closer Louis Varland who took home AL honors.

How long will we have two different Reliever of the Year awards?

First Team: Yordan Alvarez, HOU Second Team: Ben Rice, NYY

Kind of takes to the mystery out of things when you've already crowded Yordan Alvarez the Most Outstanding Designated Hitter earlier in the night...

First Team: Jacob Misiorowski, MIL First Team: Cam Schlittler, NYY First Team: Chris Sale, ATL First Team: Dylan Cease, TOR First Team: Cristopher Sánchez, PHI

Second Team: Yoshinobu Yamamoto, LAD Second Team: Sonny Gray, BOS Second Team: Tarik Skubal, DET/LAD Second Team: Drew Rasmussen, TB Second Team: Jesús Luzardo, PHI

B/R All-MLB Team Picks: Misiorowski, Schlittler, Sale, Sánchez, Cease

Another honor added to the growing list for Jacob Misiorowski and Cam Schlittler, who were already crowded Cy Young winners earlier tonight.

Edgar Martinez Outstanding Designated Hitter Award

The DH award has been given away since 1973, though it was not until 2004 that it was named after the Seattle Mariners Hall of Famer.

For the first time since 2020, someone other than Shohei Ohtani is the game's top designated hitter, and this is almost certainly an appetizer to being named AL MVP tomorrow for Yordan Alvarez.

The same guy that casually shifted from right field to shortstop and bowls 300 games in his spare time.

This is the second time Erik Neander has won this award, as he was also named Executive of the Year in 2019.

Ironically, Milwaukee Brewers president of baseball operations and general manager Matt Arnold won the award in 2024 and 2025, but had that streak snapped in the year he finally won the World Series.

AL Winner: Yordan Alvarez, Houston Astros

2025: 48 G, 118 OPS+, 6 HR, 27 RBI, 0.7 WAR 2026: 158 G, 190 OPS+, 42 HR, 106 RBI, 6.8 WAR

The likely AL MVP was a no-brainer for this award.

2025: 24 GS, 10-5, 2.71 ERA, 0.94 WHIP, 195 K, 149.2 IP 2026: 28 GS, 14-5, 3.00 ERA, 1.05 WHIP, 193 K, 162.0 IP

There's a case to be made for either guy here, especially with the strides that Elly De La Cruz made on the defensive side of the ball and with his plate discipline. But Bobby Witt Jr. is the first team pick for the third year in a row.

"Just know that you are not going to out-charisma Mookie Betts!"

Great quote from comedian Roy Wood Jr., who will once again be hosting the MLB Awards alongside the Los Angeles Dodgers star.

T-minus 15 minutes to the start of the MLB Awards.

A great combination of confidence in himself, respect for Trevor Hoffman and some laughs along the way. On a night with plenty of vanilla, stock interviews, Mason Miller brought some legitimate personality.

All-MLB Team (first and second team selections awarded, think NFL All-Pro) AL, NL Hank Aaron Award (essentially MLB's Offensive Player of the Year award) AL, NL Comeback Player of the Year Mariano Rivera (AL) & Trevor Hoffman (NL) Reliever of the Year Edgar Martinez Outstanding Designated Hitter of the Year MLB Executive of the Year

It's essentially all the awards that are not voted on by the BBWAA handed out in one night.

You read that right, Jacob Misiorowski is the first pitcher ever to win a Cy Young, a World Series ring and earn two All-Star selections over his first two seasons in the big leagues.

With the massive leap forward he took in 2026, he should be a perennial Cy Young front-runner in the years to come as he looks to make more history.

The 2026 All-MLB first and second team selections will be announced on MLB Network at 9 p.m. ET, and we assembled our own All-MLB team here at Bleacher Report a few weeks ago.

Misiorowski having roughly the same odds as Edward Cabrera (+5000) and worse odds than Spencer Schwellenbach (+3000) speaks volumes to just how much he improved in his second season in the big leagues.

Jacob Misiorowski is the presumptive winner, and there's a good chance we'll see our second unanimous Cy Young winner of the night.

It's still early days, but the 2025 deadline deal that sent Louis Varland from the Twins to the Blue Jays in exchange for Alan Roden and Kendry Rojas is shaping up to be one of the most lopsided deals in recent memory.

There's a case to be made for all three of these guys taking home the hardware, but I'll go with Tampa Bay Rays breakout star Bryan Baker for my predicted winner.

It's a unanimous Cy Young win for Schlittler, who set the bar extremely high in his first full season in the majors. What will he do for an encore in 2027?

Up next is the AL Reliever of the Year Award winner announcement.

Cam Schlittler becomes the seventh pitcher in Yankees history to win AL Cy Young honors, joining this group:

Props to the Yankees on maximizing his potential and helping him develop into a frontline starter.

A bit surprising Dylan Cease didn't get more love given his swing-and-miss stuff and the massive seven-year, $210 million contract he had just signed.

The question on the AL side isn't whether Cam Schlittler will win Cy Young honors, but if he'll do it unanimously.

Tip of the cap to Parker Messick on becoming the sixth rookie in MLB history to finish in the top three in Cy Young voting, though he seems like a lock for the No. 3 spot in the balloting.
